title: Temperature: Sensors Aren't Only Distance
description: Component lesson, brief on purpose. Not every sensor points outward — this one just needs to know how hot it is right where it sits.

content.value: Everything so far in this module answers "what's out there?" or "what's underneath?". A temperature sensor answers a much simpler question about its own immediate surroundings: how hot or cold is it right here?

A common, cheap version — a thermistor — is a resistor whose resistance changes predictably with temperature. Wire it into a simple circuit (much like Module 3's resistors) and a warmer thermistor lets more current through, a cooler one less. The controller reads that as a changing voltage and converts it to a temperature reading.

warmer  -->  thermistor resistance drops  -->  more current  -->  higher reading
cooler  -->  thermistor resistance rises   -->  less current  -->  lower reading

This is the same idea from Module 3's Ohm's law lesson, applied to a part whose resistance isn't fixed — it deliberately changes with something in the environment, which is exactly what turns a resistor into a sensor.

Key takeaway: sensors don't have to look outward. A thermistor senses its own temperature by changing its resistance predictably with heat — the same resistor-and-current relationship from Module 3, put to work as a sensor.

quiz.question: How does a thermistor let a controller measure temperature?
options: It generates its own voltage that scales with heat
Its resistance changes predictably with temperature, which changes how much current flows
quiz.explain: A thermistor is fundamentally still a resistor — just one whose resistance value is deliberately sensitive to heat.

quiz.question: What connects this lesson back to Module 3?
options: A thermistor is a resistor with a temperature-dependent resistance — the same current/resistance relationship from Ohm's law
quiz.explain: The physics is identical to any resistor circuit — the only new idea is that this resistor's value isn't fixed, it responds to heat.
